prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Iraq's government has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit to Washington amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, an Iraqi government spokesman said Tuesday. Students protest the status-of-forces agreement Tuesday at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University. Ali al-Dabbagh said the Iraqi government approved several amendments that were "necessary, essential and appropriate" to the draft status-of-forces agreement, which would set the terms for U.S. troops in Iraq after the United Nations mandate on their presence expires at the end of this year. "The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests," al-Dabbagh said. It is unclear when al-Maliki will submit the changes to the draft document. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently said that there was "great reluctance" to make any more changes to the agreement. However, senior U.S. officials -- speaking under the condition of anonymity -- are not ruling out possibly renegotiating parts of the deal with Iraq if the country's parliament does not approve it. The most vocal opponent of the draft security deal in Iraq has been the political party of radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which opposes any U.S. military presence in Iraq. U.S. military helicopters Tuesday flew over Baghdad's Mustansiriya University, where hundreds of students took part in a demonstration organized by the Sadr movement against the status-of-forces deal. "We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty," said law student Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, one of the demonstrators. Fellow demonstrator and law student Hisham Mohammed said the students plan to organize a sit-in and a strike across universities in Iraq to protest the agreement. The draft status-of-forces agreement, according to a copy obtained by CNN, calls for U.S. combat troops to be out of Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and out of the country entirely by December 31, 2011. The agreement allows for an earlier withdrawal or an extension of the U.S. forces' stay in Iraq, by agreement of both parties. It also allows the Iraqi government to ask "the United States government to leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces." Legal jurisdiction over U.S. forces in Iraq has been a sticking point in the negotiation, with the U.S. side preferring that its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. Baghdad had sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit major crimes in the course of their duties. Under the draft agreement, U.S. forces or contractors who commit "major and premeditated murders" while off duty and outside U.S. facilities would fall under Iraqi jurisdiction, according to the copy obtained by CNN. All other crimes -- and murders committed inside U.S. facilities or by on-duty forces -- would fall under American jurisdiction, the agreement says.

Students protested the status-of-forces agreement Tuesday at Baghdad’s Mustansiriya University.

Spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh said the Iraqi government had approved several amendments it deemed “necessary, essential and appropriate” to the draft status-of-forces agreement, which would establish the terms governing the presence of U.S. troops in Iraq after the United Nations mandate expires at the end of this year.

“The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests,” al-Dabbagh said.

It remains unclear when al-Maliki will submit the proposed changes. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently said there was “great reluctance” to make any further revisions to the agreement.

However, senior U.S. officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, have not ruled out the possibility of renegotiating portions of the deal if Iraq’s parliament does not approve it.

The most vocal opponent of the draft security agreement in Iraq has been the political party of radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which opposes any U.S. military presence in the country.

U.S. military helicopters flew over Baghdad’s Mustansiriya University on Tuesday as hundreds of students participated in a demonstration organized by the Sadr movement against the status-of-forces agreement.

“We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty,” said Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, a law student and one of the demonstrators.

Fellow demonstrator and law student Hisham Mohammed said the students planned to organize a sit-in and a strike at universities across Iraq to protest the agreement.

According to a copy obtained by CNN, the draft status-of-forces agreement calls for U.S. combat troops to withdraw from Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and to leave the country entirely by December 31, 2011.

The agreement permits either an earlier withdrawal or an extension of the U.S. forces’ presence in Iraq, provided both parties agree. It also allows the Iraqi government to ask “the United States government to leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces.”

Legal jurisdiction over U.S. forces in Iraq has been a sticking point in the negotiations, with the U.S. side preferring that its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law.

Baghdad had sought the authority to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes unrelated to official military operations, as well as jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit major crimes while carrying out their duties.

All other crimes—including murders committed inside U.S. facilities or by on-duty forces—would fall under American jurisdiction, the agreement states.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — Iraqi government spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh said Tuesday that Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki had been given approval to present Washington with proposed revisions to a draft security pact between Iraq and the United States.

According to al-Dabbagh, the government endorsed a number of changes it considered “necessary, essential and appropriate” to the proposed status-of-forces agreement. The pact would govern the presence of American troops in Iraq once the United Nations authorization expires at the end of this year.

Al-Dabbagh said the Cabinet had empowered al-Maliki to raise the revisions with U.S. officials so the two countries could produce an agreement that protects Iraq’s sovereignty, fundamental principles and national interests.

No date has been announced for al-Maliki to deliver the proposed changes. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently said there was “great reluctance” to revise the deal further. Nevertheless, senior American officials, who spoke anonymously, have not excluded the possibility of reopening parts of the agreement if Iraq’s parliament refuses to approve it.

The strongest Iraqi opposition has come from the political movement led by radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose party rejects any continued American military presence in the country.

On Tuesday, U.S. military helicopters passed above Baghdad’s Mustansiriya University as hundreds of students participated in a Sadr movement-organized protest against the status-of-forces pact.

Law student Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, who joined the demonstration, said the protesters opposed the agreement between the Iraqi and U.S. governments because they believed it violated Iraqi sovereignty.

Another law student taking part, Hisham Mohammed, said students intended to arrange a sit-in and organize a strike at universities throughout Iraq in opposition to the pact.

A copy of the draft obtained by CNN sets July 30, 2009, as the deadline for U.S. combat forces to withdraw from Iraqi towns and cities. It also calls for all American troops to leave Iraq by December 31, 2011.

The document permits the withdrawal to occur sooner—or allows the U.S. deployment to be extended—if both governments agree. It further gives Baghdad the option of requesting that Washington keep selected forces in Iraq to train and support Iraqi troops.

One of the most difficult issues in the negotiations has been determining which country’s courts would have authority over U.S. military personnel and contractors. American negotiators favored continued immunity from Iraqi law for both groups.

The Iraqi government, by contrast, sought the right to detain and prosecute Americans accused of offenses unrelated to authorized military activity. Baghdad also wanted jurisdiction over service members and contractors alleged to have committed serious crimes while carrying out their duties.

Under the version reviewed by CNN, Iraqi courts would have authority over U.S. troops or contractors accused of “major and premeditated murders,” but only when the alleged acts occurred while they were off duty and outside American facilities.

The draft states that American authorities would retain jurisdiction in every other case, including killings committed within U.S. installations or by personnel who were on duty.

The decision could reopen negotiations with Washington, even though U.S. officials have indicated that they are reluctant to revise a text already produced through months of difficult talks. counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed news report on the Iraqi government’s proposed changes to the U.S. security agreement, including student protests, troop withdrawal deadlines, and disputes over legal jurisdiction.
counterfactuals.output:
**Iraq Seeks Changes to U.S. Security Pact as Students Protest and Legal Disputes Persist**

**BAGHDAD — October 2008** — The Iraqi government is seeking significant revisions to a proposed security agreement that would govern the presence of American forces after the United Nations mandate expires at the end of the year. The requested changes focus on firm troop-withdrawal deadlines, Iraqi control over military operations and the question of whether U.S. personnel can be tried in Iraqi courts.

The draft accord, commonly described as a Status of Forces Agreement, would replace the U.N. authorization under which U.S.-led troops have operated in Iraq since 2003. Without a new legal framework or an extension of the mandate, American forces would lack a clear basis for conducting combat missions, detaining suspects and operating military facilities after Dec. 31.

Although Iraqi and U.S. negotiators reached a preliminary text after months of talks, Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s Cabinet declined to approve it without amendments. Iraqi officials said ministers broadly accepted the need for an agreement but wanted language that more clearly protected national sovereignty and prevented the U.S. military presence from becoming open-ended.

### Demands for binding withdrawal dates

At the center of the negotiations are deadlines for the departure of approximately 150,000 U.S. troops then stationed in Iraq.

The draft called for American combat forces to withdraw from Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, 2009, and for all U.S. forces to leave the country by Dec. 31, 2011. Iraqi leaders, however, sought firmer language establishing those dates as binding obligations rather than goals that could be altered unilaterally.

Some Iraqi officials also wanted to remove or narrow provisions that might allow the withdrawal timetable to be reconsidered. The government faced strong domestic pressure to ensure that any extension beyond 2011 could occur only at Iraq’s explicit request and through a new political decision.

Washington had long resisted setting fixed departure dates, arguing that troop levels should depend on security conditions. The improving security situation in 2008, combined with growing Iraqi opposition to a prolonged foreign presence, pushed both sides toward a timetable.

Under the proposed arrangement, Iraqi forces would gradually take responsibility for security in populated areas while U.S. troops moved to bases outside the cities. American forces would continue training and supporting Iraqi units during the transition.

### Students join public opposition

The negotiations unfolded amid protests by students and other Iraqis who said the agreement could legitimize a long-term American occupation.

Students demonstrated in Baghdad and other areas, carrying Iraqi flags and banners rejecting the pact. Many called for an immediate or clearly scheduled U.S. withdrawal and objected to provisions they believed would give American troops excessive freedom to conduct operations inside Iraq.

The protests echoed the position of Shiite cleric Moqtada al-Sadr, whose political movement organized larger anti-agreement rallies and pressed Parliament to reject any accord that compromised Iraqi sovereignty. Sadrist supporters argued that foreign forces should leave without being granted new legal protections.

Opposition was not limited to one political faction. Sunni, Shiite and Kurdish leaders all raised concerns, though their priorities differed. Some feared a rapid withdrawal could endanger recent security gains, while others worried that the draft would leave Iraq unable to control American military activities.

### Dispute over criminal jurisdiction

One of the most difficult issues was legal jurisdiction over U.S. troops and civilian personnel.

The United States sought broad protection from prosecution in Iraqi courts, particularly for actions undertaken in the course of official duties. Iraqi negotiators argued that such immunity would be politically unacceptable after incidents in which civilians were killed by American forces or private security contractors.

The emerging compromise would generally give the United States primary jurisdiction over service members acting on duty. Iraq would have jurisdiction over grave crimes committed by U.S. personnel while off duty and outside agreed American facilities.

That formula, however, left crucial questions unresolved. The two governments still had to determine who would decide whether a service member was on duty and what offenses would qualify as serious crimes. Iraqi officials sought clearer wording to prevent the United States from shielding personnel simply by classifying their conduct as part of an official mission.

The status of civilian Defense Department employees and contractors was also contested. Iraq wanted contractors to be subject to Iraqi law, especially after the 2007 Nisour Square shooting, in which guards employed by the U.S. company Blackwater killed 17 Iraqi civilians. The incident intensified demands to end the sweeping immunity contractors had enjoyed under earlier occupation-era rules.

### Control of operations and detention

Iraq also sought greater authority over U.S. military operations. Proposed revisions would require American forces to coordinate missions with the Iraqi government and would limit their ability to search homes, arrest suspects or conduct raids without Iraqi approval.

Baghdad wanted exclusive control over arrest warrants and detention decisions. Iraqi officials argued that U.S. forces should no longer be able to hold Iraqis indefinitely in American-run facilities without action by Iraqi courts.

Other disputed provisions involved U.S. use of Iraqi land, airspace and military installations. Iraqi leaders wanted assurances that the country would not be used as a base for attacks on neighboring states, a concern heightened by a U.S. raid into Syria in October 2008. Iran, which has close relations with several Iraqi political parties, also strongly opposed the agreement.

### Political and diplomatic pressure

Any final accord required approval by Iraq’s Cabinet and Parliament. Al-Maliki’s government faced the difficult task of preserving military cooperation with Washington while demonstrating that Iraq was recovering full sovereignty.

American officials warned that extensive revisions could upset the balance reached during negotiations. They also said time was running short before the U.N. mandate expired. Nevertheless, U.S. representatives indicated that they would review the Iraqi proposals rather than abandon the agreement.

The dispute left both governments with limited alternatives. Iraq could request a temporary extension of the U.N. mandate, but many Iraqi leaders opposed that option because it would continue the international legal framework associated with the occupation. A failure to reach any agreement could force the United States to curtail military operations sharply.

The controversy illustrated the competing pressures surrounding the pact: Iraqi demands for sovereignty and legal accountability, American concerns about protecting troops, fears that a rapid departure could destabilize the country, and growing public insistence on a definite end to the foreign military presence.

The final outcome would determine not only when American forces left Iraq, but also the extent of Iraqi authority over those forces during their remaining years in the country.

counterfactuals.output:
# Al-Maliki says Iraq can seek changes to U.S. security pact amid student protests

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)** — Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki defended his government’s authority to revisit the security agreement governing U.S. forces in Iraq, as demonstrators at Baghdad’s Mustansiriya University called for a complete end to the American military presence.

Al-Maliki’s authority is not a unilateral power to rewrite the pact. Under the agreement, either Iraq or the United States may request amendments, but any changes must be accepted by both governments and approved through their respective constitutional procedures. Iraq may also terminate the agreement by giving the United States one year’s written notice.

That mechanism gives Baghdad a legal route to seek new terms if security or political conditions change, while preventing either side from altering the accord on its own.

The debate spilled onto the campus of Mustansiriya University, where students and other demonstrators waved Iraqi flags and voiced opposition to the continued presence of U.S. troops. The protest reflected broader concerns that the agreement could compromise Iraqi sovereignty, despite government assurances that it established a firm timetable for the American withdrawal.

Under the pact, U.S. combat forces were required to leave Iraqi cities, towns and villages by **June 30, 2009**. All U.S. forces were to withdraw from Iraq by **December 31, 2011**, unless the two countries negotiated a separate arrangement.

The agreement also changed the legal protections enjoyed by American personnel.

Iraq received primary jurisdiction over U.S. contractors and their employees. Iraqi courts could also prosecute U.S. service members and members of the civilian component accused of serious, premeditated crimes committed outside agreed U.S. facilities and while off duty.

The United States retained primary jurisdiction over offenses committed by its personnel while on duty or inside agreed facilities. U.S. authorities were responsible for determining whether a service member had been acting in an official capacity, although the agreement provided procedures for Iraq to challenge that determination.

Supporters described the pact as a bridge between the U.N. mandate that had authorized the foreign military presence and full Iraqi sovereignty. Opponents argued that the jurisdictional limits and the continued stationing of American troops left Washington with too much influence.

For al-Maliki, the agreement was both a security framework and a political test: It set a binding withdrawal schedule, expanded Iraqi legal authority and preserved a process for renegotiation — but only with U.S. consent and the required domestic approval.
